title: Akbar's House of Worship
text:
In 1575 the Mughal emperor Akbar built a hall at his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, called the Ibadat Khana, or House of Worship. At first it hosted Thursday evening discussions among Sunni Muslim scholars. The debates soon grew bitter, as learned men quarreled and insulted each other in front of the emperor, and Akbar became disillusioned with their pride.

Over the following years he opened the discussions to others. Shia Muslims, Sufis, Hindu pandits, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and Jews took part, and in 1580 Jesuit missionaries arrived from Goa at his invitation. Akbar, who could not read, listened for hours, questioned each side and made them answer each other.

His court historian Abul Fazl describes this as a search for truth wherever it could be found. The orthodox historian Badauni, who disapproved, complained that the emperor was drifting from Islam. Both agree on what happened.

The debates helped shape Akbar's policy of sulh-i kul, or peace with all. He had already abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564 and the tax on Hindu pilgrims. He appointed Hindus to high office and ruled one of the most diverse empires of his age with relative tolerance.
lesson: Listen seriously to people who believe differently from you, and make them hear each other. Understanding grows from honest exchange, not from surrounding yourself with agreement.
people: Akbar, Abul Fazl, Abd al-Qadir Badauni
source: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Abd al-Qadir Badauni, Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh
